title: Why pruning the extremities does not pain the elements: discrete degrees of the Living Soul in the body
arc: The teaching opens with the question why a man feels no pain when his hair or nail-tips are cut but feels pain immediately when a member is cut, then resolves the question by likening the body to land and its members to trees, distinguishing those growths that bear the Living Soul from those that are mere residue grown from the impurities of food.
reading:
This chapter is a teaching about discrete degrees within the human body, framed as a question of pain. Why is it that when hair is shaved or the tips of nails are cut, the man feels nothing — yet the moment a true member is cut from the body, he is pained immediately? The chapter answers by working out a correspondence between the body and the land, and between the members and the trees that grow in it.

The spiritual point is that not every part of the natural form is on the same plane of life. The body is the ultimate of love-and-wisdom, but inside the body the discrete degrees are still operative: members proper are bearers of the Living Soul — divine truth dispersed in the natural — while the outermost growths (hair, nail-tips, the desire-arousing flesh of the surface) are residue, ultimates of ultimates, grown out from the impurities of food rather than from the soul's own substance. To cut a member is to wound something in which the soul is held; to shave a tip is to remove what was never living in the higher sense. Pain is the signal that conjunction has been violated; the absence of pain reveals the absence of soul-conjunction in those parts.

The analogy of the trees carries this further. The body is likened to the land, and the members within it to trees rooted there. Some trees, when they are cut, sprout again, grow once more, and stand fast on their feet — these correspond to members and faculties whose growth-power is from the Living Soul itself, which cannot finally be extinguished and which restores itself under influx. Other trees, once cut, do not grow again — these are the corresponding fixed members that, once severed, do not return. And there is a third class implied by the distinction: those outer growths which, when cut, regrow indefinitely and continually — the hair, the nails, the surface flesh — but whose regrowth is not a sign of life from within. They grow from "the impurities of their food," that is, from the unrefined residue of the natural process, not from the Living Soul. Their endless regrowth is the very mark of their distance from the soul; what is most external and most repeatedly replaceable is precisely what has the least of the divine in it.

Behind the medical-sounding question lies a doctrinal concern characteristic of this corpus: where exactly is the Cross of Light — the Living Soul dispersed in the natural — and where is it not? The teaching distinguishes the elements (the living members through which the Living Soul is conducted) from mere outer accretions of the flesh. To cut into the elements is to disturb the soul; to trim what grows from the impurities is no offense against the soul at all. The faculty being trained here is the discrimination (the work of separating-forth) by which the regenerate person learns which acts upon the body touch the Living Soul and which do not. The closing fragments, with their reference to "this flesh which is desire-arousing" and to growth "in the impurities of their food," confirm that the outermost flesh-and-nail layer belongs to the proprium's surface and to the natural process of digestion — not to the spiritual organism — and so its cutting is morally and pneumatically indifferent.

The lacunae are heavy in the second half, but the arc is intact: question, principle (member versus tip), analogy (body as land, members as trees), classification of trees by their response to cutting, and resolution in the doctrine that what regrows endlessly from impure food is not the Living Soul's element at all. The teaching as a whole is an exercise in reading the human body itself as a hierarchy of discrete degrees, with pain as the inward witness to where the soul truly dwells.
